title: Crowds and Collective Behavior
description: Classical theories of crowds, contagion, and the move to emergent norms

concepts.title: Le Bon and the Crowd Mind
concepts.contentHtml:
Gustave Le Bon's The Crowd: A Study of the Popular Mind (1895) launched the modern study of collective behavior. Writing in the shadow of the Paris Commune, Le Bon argued that individuals in a crowd lose their rational, civilised individuality and acquire a 'collective mind' that is impulsive, suggestible, and intellectually inferior.

His three mechanisms: anonymity (the crowd dissolves personal responsibility), contagion (emotions and ideas spread like infection), and suggestibility (the crowd enters a quasi-hypnotic state, obedient to leaders).

Gabriel Tarde's Laws of Imitation (1890) developed a parallel story in which social life as a whole is imitation cascading through populations. Together, Le Bon and Tarde set the template: crowds were treated as irrational phenomena, their participants as temporarily diminished selves. This irrationalist framing shaped a century of elite anxiety about mass politics — and a century of sociological pushback.

concepts.title: The Chicago School: Park and Blumer
concepts.contentHtml:
At the University of Chicago, Robert Park and Herbert Blumer reworked crowd theory into a more general framework of collective behavior — patterned but unstructured action that arises when shared institutions break down.

Park distinguished crowds, publics, and masses, and emphasised circular reaction: people read each other's responses and amplify a common mood. Blumer's 1939 essay set out a typology — casual crowds, conventional crowds, expressive crowds, acting crowds — and a developmental sequence: milling (restless circulation), collective excitement, social contagion.

Crucially, Blumer included social movements as a kind of collective behavior alongside fads, panics, and crazes. They were episodes of social becoming, in which new norms, identities, and institutions could emerge. The Chicago School softened Le Bon's contempt without yet abandoning the assumption that collective action was, at root, a symptom of breakdown rather than ordinary politics by other means.

concepts.title: Emergent Norm Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Ralph Turner and Lewis Killian's Collective Behavior (1957, revised 1972, 1987) attacked the irrationalist legacy directly. Crowds, they argued, are not undifferentiated emotional masses; they are populations of diverse people who appear unified because a salient norm has emerged.

In an ambiguous situation — a fire alarm, a police shooting, a stalled rally — participants look around for cues. A few visible actors define what is appropriate; others adjust. Once a definition takes hold, dissenters fall silent, comply, or leave. The crowd looks uniform, but uniformity is the product of a public norm, not a shared psychological state.

Emergent norm theory reframed crowd dynamics in the same terms as small-group sociology: people interpret situations, negotiate meaning, and respond to perceived expectations. It rehabilitated the rationality of crowd participants and pointed forward to the cognitive and cultural turns in movement studies.

title: Grievance, Resources, and Mobilization
description: From relative deprivation to the resource mobilization revolution

concepts.title: Relative Deprivation
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do people rebel? An obvious answer: because they suffer. But absolute misery rarely produces revolt — the most oppressed are often the least able to organise. Ted Robert Gurr's Why Men Rebel (1970) developed the concept of relative deprivation: the gap between what people expect to have and what they think they can have.

When expectations rise faster than capabilities — or capabilities collapse while expectations hold — frustration builds, and political violence becomes more likely. James Davies' earlier J-curve theory (1962) made a similar point: revolutions tend to follow periods of rising prosperity that are abruptly reversed.

Relative deprivation gave grievance-based explanations a more sophisticated form. Yet critics noted that grievances are nearly universal while protest is rare. Something else must explain when frustration translates into action — a puzzle that pushed sociologists toward the question of capacity rather than complaint.

concepts.title: Olson's Collective Action Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Mancur Olson's The Logic of Collective Action (1965) reframed mobilization as an economic puzzle. If a movement secures a public good — clean air, civil rights, regime change — everyone benefits whether or not they participated. Each rational individual therefore has an incentive to free ride: let others bear the costs while sharing the gains.

The result is paradoxical. Even when a group has shared interests, large groups may fail to organise. Only small groups, or groups offering selective incentives (private benefits available only to participants), can solve the problem.

Olson's argument was a body blow to the older assumption that shared interests automatically generate collective action. It also forced sociologists to take seriously the organizational question: what mechanisms — solidarity, identity, side payments, coercion — overcome the free-rider problem? Critics argue Olson underestimates moral commitment and the pleasure people take in participation, but the problem he posed remains the central analytical challenge of the field.

concepts.title: Resource Mobilization Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
John McCarthy and Mayer Zald's 'Resource Mobilization and Social Movements' (1977) inaugurated a paradigm shift. Movements, they argued, are not eruptions of breakdown but organised attempts at change that depend on resources: money, labour, expertise, media access, legitimacy.

The unit of analysis became the social movement organization (SMO) — Greenpeace, the NAACP, the Sierra Club — embedded in a wider social movement industry competing for adherents and donors. McCarthy and Zald highlighted the rise of professional movements staffed by paid activists and supported by 'conscience constituents' who bankroll causes that don't directly benefit them.

The theory accounts for puzzles grievance theory cannot: why protest waves cluster in prosperous times, why some grievances find organisational expression and others don't, and why the post-1960s landscape of foundations, NGOs, and lobbying outfits looks so different from earlier mass movements. Critics complain it underplays grassroots emotion and culture, but resource mobilization decisively moved the field from psychology to political sociology.

title: Political Process and Contentious Politics
description: Opportunities, repertoires, and the historical shape of protest

concepts.title: Political Opportunity Structure
concepts.contentHtml:
Resources matter, but so does the political environment. Doug McAdam's Political Process and the Development of Black Insurgency (1982) argued that the U.S. civil rights movement took off when a political opportunity structure opened: the decline of the Southern cotton economy, Black migration to Northern cities with the vote, Cold War pressure to address American racism, and a federal judiciary willing to rule on segregation.

Sidney Tarrow's Power in Movement (1994) generalised the framework. Opportunities expand when elites divide, allies become available, repression weakens, or institutional access widens. Movements ride these openings; when opportunities close, even resource-rich movements struggle.

Charles Tilly added the concept of regime: democratic regimes channel contention into routine forms (elections, lobbying, lawful protest), while authoritarian regimes either suppress contention or face explosive eruptions when controls fail. The political process tradition embedded movements in their wider political context, making explicit what resource mobilization left implicit.

concepts.title: Repertoires of Contention
concepts.contentHtml:
How do people protest? Charles Tilly's historical research showed that the answer is strikingly limited at any given time. Communities draw on a repertoire of contention — a known stock of forms (the petition, the march, the boycott, the strike, the sit-in) — that participants and authorities alike recognise as legitimate political action.

Repertoires change slowly and only in big jumps. The 18th-century English repertoire centred on local, particular, parochial actions: bread riots, charivari, attacks on tax collectors. Between roughly 1780 and 1850, Tilly argued, this gave way to a modular repertoire: cosmopolitan, autonomous, scalable forms — public meetings, demonstrations, special-purpose associations — usable on any issue, anywhere.

Each generation inherits and slightly innovates within the repertoire. The 1960s sit-in, the 21st-century encampment, the global climate strike: all represent recombinations of older forms. The repertoire concept reminds us that protest is a cultural achievement as much as a political one, and that what feels spontaneous is structured by deep historical inheritance.

concepts.title: Dynamics of Contention
concepts.contentHtml:
Doug McAdam, Sidney Tarrow, and Charles Tilly's Dynamics of Contention (2001) attempted a synthesis. Rather than treating revolutions, social movements, ethnic conflicts, and democratisation as separate fields, they proposed a unified study of contentious politics: episodic, public, collective interaction in which claims are advanced that bear on the interests of others, with at least one government as claimant or target.

Their methodological move was to look for shared mechanisms across cases — brokerage (a third party links previously unconnected actors), diffusion (a tactic spreads from one site to another), certification (an external authority validates a movement), repression, polarization. Concrete movements are recombinations of these basic processes.

The framework deliberately blurred boundaries: civil rights, the French Revolution, and the breakup of Yugoslavia could be analysed with the same toolkit. Critics worried this risked over-abstraction; defenders argued it finally let comparison cut across the silos that had fragmented the study of contention.

title: Frames, Identities, and Networks
description: Meaning-making, recruitment, and the cultural turn in movement studies

concepts.title: Framing Processes
concepts.contentHtml:
By the mid-1980s, structural theories felt incomplete: they explained capacity but not conviction. David Snow and Robert Benford filled the gap with framing theory. Drawing on Erving Goffman, they argued that movements actively produce schemata of interpretation — frames — that render events meaningful and motivate action.

Three core framing tasks (Snow and Benford 1988): the diagnostic frame identifies a problem and assigns blame; the prognostic frame proposes a solution and a strategy; the motivational frame supplies a rationale for action ('we' must act, 'now', because…). A successful movement frame must achieve resonance with potential supporters' existing beliefs and lived experience.

Snow's earlier work on frame alignment (1986) catalogued how movements link their frames to recruits' worldviews — by bridging compatible frames, amplifying values, extending into new domains, or transforming worldviews wholesale. Master frames (rights, equality, choice) cut across movements and cycles. Framing put meaning at the centre of mobilization.

concepts.title: New Social Movements and Identity
concepts.contentHtml:
European theorists in the 1970s and 80s — Alain Touraine, Alberto Melucci, Jürgen Habermas — argued that the post-1960s wave of feminist, environmental, peace, gay, and anti-nuclear movements differed from older labour movements in ways that demanded new theory. They labelled them new social movements (NSMs).

NSMs, on this account, are less about redistributing resources and more about identity, recognition, and cultural codes. Their participants are typically middle-class, educated, post-materialist; their organisational forms are decentralised, prefigurative, suspicious of hierarchy. Melucci's Nomads of the Present (1989) emphasised the everyday, submerged, network-based practices of meaning-making in which collective identity is constructed.

The NSM thesis has been criticised — older movements were always partly cultural, and 'new' movements still seek policy change — but it productively foregrounded collective identity as a movement product, not a precondition. Identity is something a movement actively builds and maintains, not a resource it inherits.

concepts.title: Networks, Recruitment, and High-Risk Activism
concepts.contentHtml:
How do individuals end up in movements? Doug McAdam's study of Freedom Summer (1986, 1988) tracked applicants to the 1964 voter-registration project that sent Northern volunteers to Mississippi. Many were accepted but withdrew before going. What distinguished participants from no-shows?

Two factors stood out. Biographical availability: participants had fewer constraints — no spouse, no full-time job, no dependents — that would make a dangerous summer prohibitively costly. Network embeddedness: they had stronger prior ties to others already involved in civil rights organisations and to activist networks. Attitudes alone predicted little; relationships predicted a lot.

This finding has been replicated for movements as different as Italian terrorism, religious cults, and contemporary climate activism. Movements recruit through strong ties, especially for high-risk activism; weak ties are better for diffusing information and tactics. Mobilization is therefore a network phenomenon as much as an ideological one — a finding that anchors much current empirical movement research.

title: Revolutions, Outcomes, and the Digital Era
description: Structural revolution, when movements succeed, and the Internet's mixed legacy

concepts.title: Skocpol on Social Revolutions
concepts.contentHtml:
Theda Skocpol's States and Social Revolutions (1979) compared the French (1789), Russian (1917), and Chinese (1949) revolutions. Against voluntarist accounts that stressed revolutionary ideology and leadership, she insisted: revolutions are not made; they come.

The key, on her structural account, is the state. Old-regime states collapsed under the joint pressure of international military competition they could not afford and domestic class structures (especially landlord–peasant relations) they could not reform. Once central authority cracked, peasant communities — autonomous in France, organised in communes in Russia, structured by lineages in China — could revolt effectively. Revolutionary intellectuals then competed to consolidate a new, stronger state.

Skocpol's emphasis on state breakdown and peasant insurrection shifted revolution studies decisively. Critics noted that later revolutions (Iran 1979, Eastern Europe 1989, the Arab Spring) involve urban populations and ideologies in ways her model underweights. But her demand that we ground revolutions in concrete state and class structures, rather than romantic narratives, remains foundational.

concepts.title: When Do Movements Succeed?
concepts.contentHtml:
William Gamson's The Strategy of Social Protest (1975) studied 53 American 'challenging groups' between 1800 and 1945 and asked which won. He found that movements that were narrow in goals, willing to use disruptive tactics, bureaucratically organised, and not factionalised were more likely to gain new advantages and recognition.

Edwin Amenta's later political mediation theory refined the picture: tactics that work depend on the political context. Disruption helps when allies are in office and the regime is responsive; in hostile contexts, the same tactics provoke repression. There is no universal best strategy; movements must read their political environment.

Outcomes are also multidimensional. Movements may achieve policy wins (legislation), biographical impacts (changing participants' lives), cultural shifts (the women's movement and gender norms), or institutional embedding (an industry of NGOs). The civil rights movement passed major laws; Occupy 2011 changed almost no policy yet shifted public discourse on inequality. Success has no single metric.

concepts.title: Connective Action and Its Discontents
concepts.contentHtml:
The Arab Spring of 2011, Spain's 15-M movement, Occupy Wall Street, and Black Lives Matter all spread through digital networks at speeds that older theories struggled to explain. W. Lance Bennett and Alexandra Segerberg's The Logic of Connective Action (2013) argued that personalised digital communication enables movements without the formal organisations resource mobilization theory presumed: shared content (a hashtag, an image, a slogan) becomes the connective tissue.

Yet Zeynep Tufekci's Twitter and Tear Gas (2017) cautioned against techno-optimism. Networked movements scale up faster than older movements but are tactically thinner: they reach the streets without first building the slow infrastructure — meetings, shared decisions, leadership succession — that lets a movement adapt under pressure. Authoritarian regimes have learned to flood the same platforms with disinformation, surveil organisers, and exhaust attention.

The contemporary picture is mixed. Digital tools genuinely lower coordination costs and expand who can participate. They also produce fragile mobilizations, vulnerable to repression and burnout. The deep questions of grievance, opportunity, framing, and organisation that earlier theorists posed have not gone away — they have only acquired new platforms.
